ARTICLE IN PRESS Gendered language in telephone conversations: a corpus-based study of lexical, grammatical, and pragmatic variation Abstract: Gender constitutes a central variable in studies of language variation, as it both reflects and challenges prevailing conceptions of how men and women are socialized into distinct conversational styles. The present study examines gender-related differences in spoken American English through an analysis of the Switchboard Dialogue Act CoSrpus, a large dataset comprising S 1,155 spontaneous telephone conversations involving 1,0E58 male and 1,252 female speakers. R Grounded in variationist sociolinguistics, a corpus-bPased quantitative approach was employed to N identify gender-related patterns across lexical, grammatical, and pragmatic dimensions. The I E analysis revealed that women produced significantly more turns and utterances, whereas men L C produced longer utterances and lexical items. Lexically, both genders shared most vocabulary, I T though notable contrasts Remerged: men more frequently used uh, while women preferred um; A women also employed we and family-related terms more often, whereas men used wife with higher frequency. Grammatically, men showed a preference for nouns, numerals, and determiners, while women favored pronouns, verbs, and the to-infinitive form. Pragmatically, men tended to use statement-opinion, whereas women were more inclined toward statement-non-opinion. Contrary to earlier claims, no significant gender difference was observed in the use of tag questions. These findings demonstrate that gender differences in spoken language are real yet subtle, highly context- dependent, and best captured through large-scale corpus evidence rather than through stereotypical assumptions or broad generalizations. Introduction This study investigates gender-related variation in spoken English, a topic that has been extensively explored in certain respects (Hancock & Rubin, 2015). Its primary aim is to identify the linguistic features that differentiate the speech of women and mSen across lexical, grammatical, S and pragmatic levels. Previous research has generally Echaracterized women’s language as R exhibiting a higher frequency of hedges, tag questioPns, intensifiers, pronouns, fillers, politeness N forms, and minimal responses (Lakoff, 1975; McMillan et al., 1977; Hirschman, 1994; Mulac & I E Lundell, 1986; Singh, 2001; Leaper & Ayres, 2007; Menz & Al-Roubaie, 2008; Palomares, 2008; L C Stubbe, 2013; Fuchs, 2017; Hessner & Gawlitzek, 2017). Men, by contrast, have been found to I T produce longer utterancesR, employ longer words, and display higher type–token ratios (Pillon et A al., 1992; Singh, 2001). These conclusions have been drawn from data collected across a wide range of communicative contexts, including laboratory experiments (e.g., Bortfeld et al., 2001), workplace interactions (e.g., Holmes, 2005), computer-mediated communication (e.g., Thomson, 2006), criminal proceedings (e.g., Waara & Shaw, 2006), medical interviews (e.g., Menz & Al- Roubaie, 2008), and doctor–patient consultations (e.g., Sandhu et al., 2009). Additional studies have examined gender differences in advice-giving (e.g., Al-Shboul & Abumahfouz, 2018) and apology expressions (e.g., Jones & Adrefiza, 2017). Consequently, there is no clear consensus, as different contexts influence the use of ARTICLE IN PRESS linguistic variables by women and men (Leaper & Ayres, 2007; Hancock & Rubin, 2015; Plug et al., 2021; Piersoul & Van de Velde, 2023). As Hancock and Rubin (2015, p. 2) observe, “men were more talkative overall, especially in disagreement or nonpersonal conversations, yet women were more talkative with classmates, dating partners, and in parent-child interactions.” Moreover, many earlier investigations were conducted in university laboratory settings, where participants assumed conversational roles that rarely occur in natural environments (Leaper & Ayres, 2007). Role-play conversations differ markedly from auSthentic exchanges (Tsui, 1994; S Baker, 2014). Piersoul and Van de Velde (2023) refer Eto the use of artificial data, which R compromises ecological validity. Gender differenPces in spoken language therefore remain N insufficiently explored. I E Sociolinguistic research based on authentic spoken corpora remains limited, largely due to L C the scarcity of large spoken language sources (Baker, 2014; Baker & Heritage, 2022). Compared I T with the many studies focRusing on written texts (Biber et al., 1998; Koppel et al., 2002; Newman A et al., 2008; Cheng et al., 2011; Tang, 2021), relatively few have systematically investigated gendered speech patterns using spoken corpus data. Furthermore, these studies have primarily focused on lexical gender differences (Rayson et al., 1997; Kilgarriff, 2001; Schmid, 2003; Baker, 2014) rather than on grammatical or pragmatic aspects. The present study addresses this gap by analyzing a large corpus of everyday telephone conversations, the Switchboard Dialogue Act Corpus (SwDA). As Baker (2014) notes, corpus methods yield more reliable insights by combining extensive datasets with automated searches of diverse linguistic phenomena. This paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews relevant ARTICLE IN PRESS literature; Section 3 describes the data and methodology; Section 4 presents the findings; Section 5 discusses their implications; and Section 6 provides concluding remarks. 2. Methodology This section first describes the corpus data employed in the study, then outlines the data processing procedures and the analytical framework. ARTICLE IN PRESS 3.1. Corpus Resources During the data selection process, rigorous measures were implemented to ensure that the selected corpus accurately represented the linguistic usage patterns across both genders. The Switchboard Dialogue Act Corpus (SwDA) was therefore selected instead of the British National Corpus (BNC) to obtain data that consistently reflects gender differences while controlling for other variables. The Switchboard Dialogue Act (SwDA) Corpus 3 comprises 1,155 transcribed telephone conversations, totaling 223,606 lines of transcripts and approximSately 1.5 million word tokens S (Fang et al., 2011). The SwDA corpus was chosen for threeE reasons. R First, it consists of data spontaneously produPced by English speakers in natural contexts. N The telephone conversations span a wide range of everyday topics—such as hobbies, weather, I E employment, education, pollution, and crime—making it a general-domain corpus. L C Second, the conversations are richly annotated to capture distinctive features of spoken I T language. Each turn is seRgmented into utterances, referred to as “slash units” (Meteer & Taylor, A 1995). Within these utterances, restarts and non-sentential elements are marked, including fillers ({F…}), discourse markers ({D…}), and coordinating conjunctions ({C…}). In addition, all utterances have been manually annotated with dialogue act (DA) information according to the SWBD-DAMSL coding scheme (Jurafsky et al., 1997), an extension of the Discourse Annotation and Markup System of Labeling (DAMSL). The SWBD-DAMSL scheme, comprising 60 basic labels, provides a framework for annotating communicative functions within utterances. Its primary purpose is to label Switchboard conversations for training stochastic discourse grammars, thereby improving language models (LMs) for automatic speech recognition (ASR). ARTICLE IN PRESS Third, telephone conversations constitute an ideal data source for investigating linguistic features because they offer rich verbal data in the absence of nonverbal cues (Heinz, 2003). In face-to-face interaction, nonverbal cues such as gaze, gesture, and touch can influence verbal expression. By contrast, telephone conversations provide a more controlled yet authentic environment for examining natural language use in interactive speech. In addition, the files labeled “transcript summaries” contain meta-information about the two participants in each conversation, including gender informaStion, accessible via LDC97S62 S (https://catalog.ldc.upenn.edu/LDC97S62). These metadataE were integrated into the present study R so that gender information could be matched to eachP conversation. In comparing men and women, both the effect size and statistical significance (p-value) were considered, given that p-values are sensitive to sample size. A statistically significant gender difference (typically p < 0.05) does not necessarily imply a meaningful difference in practical terms. To measure the effect size of the mean difference between women and men, Cohen’s d was calculated by dividing the mean difference by the pooled standard deviation (Cohen, 1988). The log-likelihood (LL) test, computed from raw frequency data, is designed to handle large quantities of non-parametric data and is particularly suited to assessing the statistical significance of differences in token counts for specific linguistic features across corpora (Dunning, 1993). In this study, the LL test was applied to compare word-token frequencies and to analyze differences in word-class and communicative-function distributions. 3.3. Framework for analysis The analytic approach adopted in this research falls within the framework of empirical linguistics, ARTICLE IN PRESS specifically variationist sociolinguistics, which belongs to the descriptive-interpretative strand of modern linguistic inquiry. The variationist method relies on quantitative analysis to validate data interpretations, to reveal the sociocultural significance of linguistic variation, and to capture the probabilistic nature of relationships among linguistic features. Quantitative analysis offers a more accurate account of usage and frequency within the community, while the distribution of forms and speakers’ preferences provides a realistic depiction of linguistic structures in practice. Crucially, statistical tools make it possible to identify Sboth the social and linguistic S conditioning of forms and the regularities that underlie the syEstem. As a more objective and reliable R basis for analysis than intuition or value judgments, tPhe quantitative method is both powerful and N efficient. Corpora, in turn, provide an ideal foundation for such investigation. This study employs I E a corpus of telephone conversations to uncover discourse patterns in men’s and women’s speech L C that remain largely inaccessible through introspection. Within the corpus, recurrent patterns that I T constitute grammatical strRuctures are revealed through co-occurrence frequencies. A 4. Results 4.1. Discussion Gender is a key social variable in studies of language variation, and research on gender differences in spoken language use provides valuable insights into the nature of language itself. Our results demonstrate that men and women express themselves differently, though they exhibit more similarities than differences at the lexical level. Greater variation emerges in grammatical categories, while at the pragmatic level, the numbeSr of significantly different and S similar communicative functions is roughly equivalent.E A comprehensive understanding of R gendered language use thus requires large spoken corPpora. N Overall, our results are broadly consistent with earlier findings, though some important I E differences appear. Regarding speech quantity, women produced significantly more turns and L C utterances, whereas men produced significantly longer utterances and words. In other words, I T women spoke more oftenR, while men spoke in longer stretches. The gender difference in mean A utterance length emerges as the most salient, whereas differences in the average number of words and mean turn length are negligible. These findings suggest that observable gender variation manifests primarily in utterance length, while differences in turn length or overall word count are minimal. These findings partly align with studies suggesting that men tend to speak more than women (Crawford, 1995; Easton, 1994; see James & Drakich, 1993, for review), particularly when measured in terms of utterance or phrase length (Pillon et al., 1992; Hannah & Murachver, 2007; Singh, 2001; Leaper & Ayres, 2007). However, other studies have reported the reverse pattern. ARTICLE IN PRESS Several factors may account for these discrepancies. First, many earlier studies relied on small datasets (Newman et al., 2008; Yu, 2014), which may limit representativeness and produce inconsistent results. Secondly, as noted in Section 1, many of these studies are based on data drawn from diverse institutional settings, and some scholars (e.g., Baker, 2014) have argued that conversational context can significantly influence the use of linguistic variables. Thirdly, Plug et al. (2021) emphasize that differing operationalizations—some studies measuring total word counts and others mean utterance length—complicate cross-study compSarisons and may partly explain S the inconclusive results reported in the literature. E R Across linguistic levels, the features showingP the most pronounced gender differences— N uh, nouns, and statement-opinion—occur significantly more frequently among men. This pattern I E suggests that the most salient gender differences in our corpus are male-dominant. Specifically, uh L C is dramatically more frequent in men’s speech, whereas um occurs more often among women. I T Clark and Tree (2002) demRonstrated that uh typically precedes shorter pauses than um. This finding A suggests that women may anticipate needing slightly more time for cognitive processing during interaction. In contrast, men prefer uh, implying that they expect to require only a brief moment for cognitive retrieval. From this perspective, the findings suggest that women are more conservative and less confident than men, as they seem to need additional time to process their thoughts. Moreover, the pronoun we exhibits the strongest gender difference observed, yet this feature has been largely overlooked in previous research. The inclusive we appears to convey a sense of collective experience, and women use it significantly more frequently, possibly to establish a ARTICLE IN PRESS stronger connection with their conversational partner. With respect to word classes, the gender differences observed in this study are consistent with those reported by Biber et al. (1998) for written texts. Biber (1995) employed part-of-speech patterns to develop an index of text types distinguishing between “involved” language (e.g., frequent use of pronouns and present-tense verbs) and “informational” language (e.g., higher frequencies of nouns and longer words). Based on written data, Biber et al. found that female language tended to be more involved, whereas male languageS was more informational. Our S findings further support this distinction. Since to-infinitive Econstructions are often used to express R “intentions, desires, efforts, perceptual states, and variPous other general actions” (Biber et al., 2021, N p. 686), women use them significantly more frequently. This suggests that women are more I E inclined to articulate intentions and desires, thereby participating more actively in interaction. By L C contrast, men make greater use of the existential there construction to convey information more I T efficiently. R A Regarding the communicative functions performed by each utterance, our findings support previous research suggesting that men use language instrumentally to convey information, whereas women are more likely to use it for social connections (Newman et al., 2008). This pattern is evident in our corpus, where men prefer a wider range of question and answer types, while women employ more backward communicative functions. One notable divergence from previous literature concerns tag questions, traditionally regarded as a hallmark of female language. In our data, tag questions did not differ significantly by gender. Women produced more statement-non-opinion utterances, while men favored ARTICLE IN PRESS statement-opinion, suggesting that in everyday telephone conversations men tend to be more assertive in expressing personal viewpoints. It is important to be cautious when making claims about female politeness, as only a few politeness strategies—such as conventional-closing and conventional-opening—were used more frequently by women. No significant gender differences were found in other politeness-related functions, including thanking and apology. Therefore, it would be unwarranted to generalize that women are inherently more polite than men. S S 6. Conclusion E R Despite a considerable number of studies basedP on institutional interactions, laboratory N experiments, and questionnaires, there remains a lack of comprehensive understanding of how I E women and men use language in everyday telephone conversations. Previous research using L C spoken corpora has mainly focused on individual linguistic dimensions—such as lexical items, I T specific words, word claRsses, or communicative functions—and thus provides only a partial A perspective on the relationship between gender and language use. By contrast, the present study analyzed a large spoken corpus to offer a broader overview of gendered language use. In doing so, it demonstrates how corpus-based analysis can contribute to a more nuanced and comprehensive understanding of spoken language and gender. This study has examined gender-related differences in spoken American English using the Switchboard Dialogue Act Corpus, a large dataset comprising 1,155 spontaneous telephone conversations involving 1,058 men and 1,252 women. The analysis encompassed lexical, grammatical, and pragmatic dimensions. The results show that women produced significantly ARTICLE IN PRESS more turns and utterances, whereas men produced longer utterances and words. At the lexical level, both genders shared most of their vocabulary, yet clear contrasts emerged: men favored uh, while women preferred um; women also used we and family-related terms more often, whereas men used wife more frequently. Grammatically, men favored nouns, numerals, and determiners, while women used more pronouns, verbs, and to-infinitive constructions. Pragmatically, men were more likely to employ statement-opinion, whereas women favored statement-non-opinion. Contrary to earlier claims, no significant gender difference was found in the uSse of tag questions. Overall, the S findings indicate that gender differences in spoken languaEge are real but subtle, highly context- R dependent, and best understood through large-scPale corpus analyses rather than through N stereotypes or broad generalizations. I E Ultimately, it must be emphasized that the differences in language use between men and L C women are not unambiguous, as language is shaped by other, less easily measurable factors such I T as context, economic statuRs, and the balance of power between speakers, as noted by Eckert (2012), A Eckert and McConnell-Ginet (2003), and Cameron (2007). It should also be acknowledged that the dialogues analyzed in the present study were collected in the 1990s, and linguistic patterns may have shifted since then. Consequently, the gender differences discussed here may not fully reflect present-day usage. However, perfectly balanced data—especially large-scale corpora annotated with pragmatic information—remain rare. Under such circumstances, the best we can do is to describe linguistic reality as accurately and comprehensively as possible. JSON: Name: gendered_telephone_corpus_pipeline Title: A corpus-based quantitative pipeline to measure gender effects on lexical, grammatical, and pragmatic variation in spontaneous telephone conversations Short Hypothesis: Controlling for conversational topic and interlocutor familiarity, speaker gender causally affects the distribution of filled pauses (um vs. uh), mean utterance length, part-of-speech frequencies, and dialogue-act type frequencies in spontaneous telephone conversations. Related Work: Prior approaches split into small-scale experimental/role-play studies and corpus-based observational analyses. Experimental work yields controlled manipulations but limited ecological validity and small samples. Corpus-based lexical studies (keyword lists, intensifier/swear-word counts) leveraged medium-sized spoken corpora (often the BNC spoken component) to find gender-linked preferences for fillers, intensifiers, and topical vocabulary, but these studies commonly: (1) used heterogeneous corpora combining dialogues, monologues, and institutional speech, producing context confounds; (2) focused primarily on lexical items rather than jointly modeling grammatical and pragmatic layers; (3) relied on raw frequency comparisons without mixed-effects controls for topic, speaker, or conversation-level random effects; and (4) applied inconsistent operationalizations of ‘talkativeness’ (total words vs. turns vs. utterance length). Dialogue-act annotated corpora exist (e.g., SwDA) but have been underused for gender analyses and cross-corpus generalization. These limitations leave unresolved questions about whether reported gender differences reflect speaker gender per se or contextual and sampling biases. Abstract: This pipeline operationalizes a reproducible, corpus-based methodology to test whether speaker gender systematically influences lexical, grammatical, and pragmatic features in spontaneous telephone conversations. Using a primary dialogue-act annotated telephone corpus and two held-out spoken corpora, the pipeline (1) aligns speaker metadata with transcripts and POS/DA annotations, (2) computes normalized lexical and grammatical distributions and STTR measures, and (3) fits mixed-effects regression models and predictive classifiers that control for topic, interlocutor familiarity, and conversation-level random effects. The main contribution is an end-to-end, statistically rigorous workflow that jointly evaluates filled pauses (um vs. uh), utterance length, POS-class shifts, and dialogue-act frequencies while measuring effect sizes and cross-corpus generalization. Expected outcomes include quantification of which features show robust gender-linked variation after controlling for confounds, estimates of practical effect sizes, and an evaluation of how corpus choice and contextual controls affect replicability. The pipeline is intended to produce defensible, reproducible claims about gender-related language variation in telephone interactions. Experiments: Datasets: Primary: Switchboard Dialogue Act Corpus (SwDA) full set (1,155 conversations; ~1.5M tokens); Tagged subset for POS: Penn-Treebank-tagged SwDA subset (1,126 dialogues, ~1.5M tokens). Secondary/held-out corpora for generalization: Spoken BNC conversation component (1994 and 2014 subsets), Corpus of Spoken Professional American English (CSPAE) or comparable telephone/face-to-face spoken corpora where available. Preprocessing: align speaker gender metadata, normalize tokens (lowercase, preserve disfluency markers), use existing POS/DA annotations when available; when absent, run a conversational-aware POS tagger and DA classifier. Feature sets: (A) Lexical: normalized token frequencies per million, STTR (1000-token sampling); (B) Fillers: counts of 'um' and 'uh' and orthographic variants; (C) Grammatical: POS tag frequencies and to-infinitive/existential-there counts; (D) Pragmatic: DA-type frequencies. Baselines: (1) Null statistical model (no gender predictor); (2) Logistic/multinomial regression using only lexical features; (3) Random forest classifier on combined features; (4) Mixed-effects linear models for continuous outcomes (utterance length) with random intercepts for speaker and conversation. Statistical tests and metrics: mixed-effects model coefficients with p-values and 95% CIs; Cohen's d for effect sizes; log-likelihood ratio tests for token frequency differences; for classifiers: accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC; calibration plots. Experimental protocol: (1) Replication study on SwDA: fit mixed-effects models predicting each dependent variable (filled-pause choice, utterance length, POS proportions, DA counts) with fixed effect speaker gender and covariates topic label, interlocutor familiarity indicator; random intercepts for speaker and conversation. (2) Ablation study: compare models with (a) no context controls, (b) topic control only, (c) topic + familiarity controls, (d) add interaction terms gender×topic; measure changes in coefficient magnitude and statistical significance. (3) Feature ablation classification: train gender classifiers on SwDA using lexical-only, POS-only, DA-only, combined; report performance and feature importance; evaluate drop in performance when removing each feature class. (4) Cross-corpus generalization: train models on SwDA, test on Spoken BNC subset and CSPAE; report transfer drop (delta AUC/accuracy) and repeat mixed-effects tests on each corpus. Multiple-comparison correction: Benjamini–Hochberg FDR for token-level LL tests. Repetition: 5-fold cross-validation over conversations for classifier experiments; bootstrapped CIs (1,000 resamples) for regression estimates. Risk Factors and Limitations: Data bias: SwDA and legacy corpora are region- and era-specific (US speakers from 1990s), limiting temporal, regional, and socio-demographic representativeness; gender is recorded as a binary label, excluding nonbinary identities and risking misgendering. Topic and role confounds: imperfect topic labels and missing interlocutor-familiarity metadata can leave residual confounding. Annotation noise: POS and dialogue-act tags may contain errors; automated tagging for secondary corpora introduces additional label noise. Small practical effects: large corpora can yield statistically significant but practically negligible differences (small Cohen's d), complicating interpretation. Imbalanced samples: unequal counts of male/female speakers require normalization and increase variance of some estimates. Cross-corpus generalization failure: models may not transfer due to register, recording conditions, or annotation schema differences. Ethical/legal: speaker metadata privacy concerns and licensing restrictions may limit data sharing. Computational limits: mixed-effects models with large token-level datasets and many random effects may be computationally expensive or fail to converge. Causal inference limits: observational design supports conditional association testing but cannot fully establish causality beyond controlled experiments.
